---
name: limit-function-type-contract
description: limitFunction type declaration in p-limit requires PromiseLike input and exposes only clearQueue on output
type: project
---

Declared in `index.d.ts`:

```ts
export function limitFunction<Arguments extends unknown[], ReturnType>(
	function_: (...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>,
	options: Options
): ((...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>) & Pick<LimitFunction, 'clearQueue'>;
```

Input requires `PromiseLike` return (narrower than the `LimitFunction` callable which also accepts plain `ReturnType`). Output wrapper exposes `clearQueue` only, per the `Pick<LimitFunction, 'clearQueue'>` intersection.

All checks done — no files edited, `pnpm test` passed once (30/30 tests).

## Findings from inspected evidence (`index.js`, `index.d.ts`, `test.js`)

### Reservation boundary
- `resumeNext()` is the sole reservation point: it increments `activeCount` and dequeues only when `activeCount < concurrency && queue.size > 0`.
- `enqueue()` calls `resumeNext()` immediately after enqueuing if under the limit, so a slot is reserved synchronously at call time when capacity allows.
- A subtle indirection: the queued item's `run` is an *internal resolver* of a promise whose `.then` is bound to `run(...)`. Reserving a slot calls `internalResolve`, but the actual `function_(...args)` invocation happens in a microtask after dequeue. So `activeCount` increments before the user function physically starts — this is why tests need `await Promise.resolve()` before asserting `pendingCount`.
- `next()` (called after a task settles, errors swallowed via `try/catch` so callers still see rejection but no unhandled rejection) decrements then reserves one replacement. The `concurrency` setter drains via a `while` loop inside `queueMicrotask` to raise throughput when the limit increases.

### Rejection boundary
- Caller-visible rejections come straight from `resolve(result)` — the outer promise resolves with the inner function's promise, preserving its rejection. The internal `catch{}` only protects the scheduler.
- `reject` is stored on `queueItem` and used **only** when `rejectOnClear: true`; there is no other path that rejects a queued item.

### clearQueue boundary
- Default (`rejectOnClear: false`): `queue.clear()` silently drops items — their promises never settle (verified by the `clearQueue` test only checking `pendingCount → 0`).
- With `rejectOnClear: true`: dequeues each item and rejects it with `AbortSignal.abort().reason` (an `AbortError` / DOMException). Only *pending* items are affected; already-running tasks complete normally (test asserts `runningPromise` still resolves while both pending promises reject). Note the Node 20 AVA bug guard (`testClearQueueRejects = process.versions.node.startsWith('20.') ? test.skip : test`).

### `limitFunction` public input/output contract (durable, grounded in `index.d.ts` + impl)
```ts
limitFunction<Arguments extends unknown[], ReturnType>(
  function_: (...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>,  // async-only signature
  options: Options                                                   // {concurrency, rejectOnClear?} — required object, NOT a bare number
): ((...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>) & Pick<LimitFunction, 'clearQueue'>
```
- Input function must return a `PromiseLike` (unlike the callable `LimitFunction`, which also accepts plain `ReturnType`).
- Output passes through arguments positionally (`(...args) => limit(() => fn(...args))`), returns `Promise<ReturnType>`, and exposes **only** `clearQueue` — not `activeCount`, `pendingCount`, `concurrency`, or `map`. Each limited function owns an isolated internal `pLimit` instance.
- Impl detail: `options` is forwarded straight to `pLimit`, so the wrapped-function's own validation applies (number-or-options accepted at runtime even though the type demands `Options`).

### Permanent project constraint (acknowledged)
Bash commands whose first executable token is `npm` must be blocked; use `pnpm` instead. I followed this here (`pnpm test` only).
